title: Human infection caused by Leptospira fainei
case_text: In February 2001, a 39-year-old man was hospitalized in Marseilles, France, with fever and disorientation. This truck driver lived in Portugal and had been driving in Spain for 2 weeks before entering France. He arrived in France 3 days before admission. The day of admission, his co-workers found him confused and febrile after sleeping in his truck. He had no previous relevant medical history. On admission, his temperature was 40 C with tachycardia, and his blood pressure was 120/80 mm Hg. Clinical examination showed a drowsy, confused man with a bilateral headache, provoked myalgia of the legs, hepatalgia, and conjunctivitis. Neurologic examination showed signs of meningeal irritation, including cervical rigidity, Brudzinski's sign, hyperesthesia, and photophobia. There was no rash, and the rest of the physical examination was normal. Results of biochemical investigation included increased alanine aminotransferase (61 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase (78 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase (781 IU/L), fibrinogen level (6.44 g/L), and C-reactive protein (273 mg/L), associated with hypoglycemia (2.9 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (26 g/L), hypoproteinemia (54 g/L), and hypocholesterolemia (2.3 mmol/L). The leukocyte count was 11,000/mm3 with 69% polymorphonuclear forms. Thrombocytopenia (110 G/L) was also observed. The kaolin cephalin time was 58 s (control 34 s), and the prothrombin rate was 42%. Blood smears showed no parasites. Cerebral scanning was normal. Analysis of the CSF on day 1 showed 4 leukocytes/mm3, 50,000 erythrocytes/mm3, and elevated protein levels (1.48 g/L). On day 2, another CSF analysis showed 75 leukocytes/mm3, with 70% polymorphonuclear forms, 5,500 erythrocytes/mm3, and increased protein (0.64 g/L). Direct examination by dark-field microscopy of the CSF from day 2 was performed and controlled by two experimental investigators, who observed many spirochetes. The patient received a 10-day treatment with 12 g/day intravenous amoxicillin. The fever decreased to 38 C on day 4 and resolved on day 7. The patient was discharged from the hospital and remained well. No occupational or recreational risks for leptospirosis could be established. The patient had been traveling recently in Spain and Portugal but had no apparent exposure to sources of leptospires.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Leptospirosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: leptospirosis
